items.title: Beyond survival: Gaza’s children with disabilities need a chance to recover
items.summary: As Israel’s genocide in Gaza enters its fourth year, children who have lost limbs face scarce prosthetics and restricted medical supplies. A local village offers care—but recovery requires more. As Israel’s genocide in Gaza enters its fourth year, its impact continues to shape the lives of children with disabilities, particularly those who have lost limbs. Surviving the bombardment is only the first step in a long road to recovery, one that requires medical care, rehabilitation, education, and psychosocial support. In Gaza, a child might dream of walking to school, playing football with friends, or riding a bike without help. But for children who have lost limbs during the war, these simple childhood activities have become goals that depend on access to medical care, rehabilitation, and continued support. Surviving the bombardment is only the first step in a long road to recovery, one that requires medical care, rehabilitation, education, and psychosocial support. Local initiatives and humanitarian organizations are working to meet children’s immediate needs, but a larger question remains: how can these children begin to rebuild their lives when medical resources are scarce and Israel continues to restrict the entry of essential medical equipment and supplies into Gaza?

items.title: Designing durable systems: Lessons from the fight for transitional housing in Georgia
items.summary: Working in the context of Atlanta’s housing crisis, a nonprofit leader reflects on why transitional housing should be treated as a crucial step towards building a secure future for families. This article is part of South at 250, a special #WeTheCivic: America 250 series that explores how people across the region have confronted systems of exclusion and built lasting foundations for freedom. You can read more articles about communities shaping the South’s future and expanding what democracy can mean for us all here. Over time, I have come to understand that rebuilding a life takes more than encouragement or an opportunity—it takes access to resources, a stable environment, accountability, and a realistic path forward. That understanding is at the heart of why I founded YahCare Homes Inc. in Atlanta, Georgia. Our work focuses on transitional housing and supportive resources for pregnant women, mothers, and families experiencing homelessness, while our community programs respond to immediate needs that can make daily life more manageable. Georgia’s housing challenges make this work especially urgent. The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development’s 2024 Point-in-Time count recorded 12,290 people experiencing homelessness statewide on a single night, including 2,728 people in families with children. A one-night count cannot capture everyone who moves between temporary stays, doubled-up housing, motels, vehicles, or other unstable situations, but it offers a clear snapshot of the need. The National Low Income Housing Coalition also reports a shortage of more than 203,000 rental homes that are affordable and available to Georgia’s extremely low-income households.

items.title: Can a deck of cards interrupt bias in grantmaking?
items.summary: How can a deck of cards help grant reviewers challenge assumptions and create space for reflection and more equitable funding decisions? In a simpler world, worthwhile justice work would always result in a compelling grant application. But in reality, a polished grant application more often proves that an organization has an experienced grant writer, knows the language of philanthropy, and understands how to translate its work into the format a funder expects. As a result, many worthy causes fall by the wayside because grantwriting skills are one of the most influential factors determining who gets funded. This reality was not lost on the Vancouver Foundation, which was grappling with a troubling pattern in its grantmaking process: Indigenous organizations were underrepresented among recipients of its systems change grant. The grant itself was intended to help communities address systemic inequality, which made the inequity within its selection process especially important to understand. An unintentionally biased selection process was rewarding other organizations for their fluency in philanthropy’s systems and language. I spoke to service designer Ayushi Jain, who worked with social impact design studio InWithForward as part of an extensive research and design process examining how organizations experienced Vancouver Foundation’s grant method. She recalls 11 workshops and more than 60 conversations with community members.

items.title: A campaign saying ‘NO MORE’ to a violent and corrupt prison system in Alabama
items.summary: One year after The Alabama Solution, the fight for prison accountability reveals what it takes to turn public attention into political pressure—and how far Alabama still has to go. More than 1,500 people have died in Alabama’s prisons since the Justice Department declared the system unconstitutional in 2019. Homicides are more than seven times the national prison average; overdoses inside run at 13 times the statewide rate. Meanwhile, the state budgeted more than a billion dollars on a single new mega prison, even though prisons already consume nearly a quarter of the general fund—more than Alabama spends on public health and mental health combined. None of this is in dispute. It is the documented condition of a system the state has understood for years and declined to fix. Last fall, the documentary The Alabama Solution brought that condition to a national audience. We spent the year that followed on the less cinematic work behind the film: converting attention into pressure that could outlast a news cycle and reach people with the power to act. That is the work worth examining, because the field talks endlessly about raising awareness and almost never about the narrative infrastructure required to empower voices with hope and dignity in order to reach audiences for action. We treated the film as a beginning, not an achievement. Alongside the moral case, we pressed the fiscal one, which is just as true and reaches different people.

items.title: How can nonprofits do more with less? Try addressing multiple issues at once
items.summary: What does it take to look beyond single-issue solutions at a time when funding is down and the demand for help is greater than ever? In an era when needs are growing while funding is harder to come by, nonprofits are feeling the pressure to do more with less. One potential tactic is “multisolving” or addressing multiple interconnected issues from different sectors, with one program. Multisolving can mean having a wider-reaching impact, but it involves more than just tacking additional goals onto an existing program. To get it right, organizations need to identify where their work can make the greatest impact, secure flexible funding, and work closely with the communities they serve. In Tucson, Arizona, Iskashitaa Refugee Network multisolves through food initiatives. Each week, refugees connected with the organization harvest around 3,000 pounds of produce that might otherwise go to waste: fruits and vegetables from residential trees, community gardens, and other public property. Some of that produce goes home with the refugees to help stave off food insecurity, while the rest is preserved at monthly workshops and then sold in an online shop. The proceeds are then reinvested into the harvesting program. With one action, Iskashitaa addresses food waste and food insecurity, while also helping refugees connect with each other and with the broader community.

items.title: Soul work: What it takes to build democracy from the ground up
items.summary: Amid ICE raids and DEI rollbacks, building democracy from the ground up requires relational, unglamorous work—cross-sector partnerships, trust, and community infrastructure that no executive order can dismantle. NPQ’s column, We Stood Up, features first-person stories from workers, builders, activists, and organizers of their work and world. From inspirational stories to strategic insights and powerful solutions, these stories may offer a moment to breathe, collective wisdom, and the community solidarity we need to keep pushing toward a just and equitable future. My college friend of over 20 years and I hesitated before walking to a local Mexican restaurant. Not because of anything we had done. Not because we weren’t known in our community. We are both college educated, post-graduate degree holders, business owners, and longtime community advocates. We hesitated because of ICE raids in our city. Around us, the fear was visible and specific. The restaurant owner down the street had started preparing meals for neighbors too afraid to leave their homes and delivering food to the local car wash, where workers had no choice but to show up but were terrified to step outside. My friend runs a speech therapy clinic where most of her clients are Latinx undocumented immigrants. Her waiting room had gone quiet. That was the first time in my life I felt truly othered. In my own community. In a city I had spent years pouring myself into. “This is what democracy actually looks like. Not the podium. The room nobody photographed. The phone call nobody reimbursed.”

items.title: American farmers’ politics are more complicated than headlines suggest
items.summary: Michael Shepherd studies the politics of rural communities. How does he think about farmers as voters? Farming 250, A Series with Civil Eats focuses on the question is being asked: What does America look like right now? In this new series, Farming 250, Civil Eats seeks to answer that question from the soil up. The newsroom is partnering with NPQ for the #WeTheCivic America 250 campaign. A predominant political narrative in both the Beltway and mainstream media posits that all American farmers voted for Trump and are now suffering due to tariffs and the Iran war. According to this narrative, the big question is whether these salt-of-the-earth, Midwestern drivers of oversized tractors will stick with the president. Michael Shepherd, an assistant professor at the University of Michigan who studies the politics of rural communities, is currently working on a farmer-focused survey that seeks to answer that exact question. But he’s also interested in how it fits into the bigger, long-term picture that gets less attention: Like most Americans, farmers have always been a diverse, complicated group with evolving political priorities. “I very much see farmers as part of this broader story of rural politics,” Shepherd told Civil Eats recently. Those politics have shifted right over the last 50 years as economic realities changed and political parties began homing in on culture war issues.

items.title: Feeling only one part of the AI elephant
items.summary: AI is pulling on every thread that runs through nonprofit missions. We must understand the full picture before accepting AI as inevitable. When I was a kid, I’d watch my mom drive and try to figure out why pressing a pedal made the whole car move. Her foot went down and the car went forward, but whatever connected the two was hidden from me, so I had to piece it together by understanding how the parts worked together. Every system is a chain of distinct causes and effects, and most of the links sit out of sight, but understanding the whole of a system is a requisite skill for the social sector. Even if most of these connections are not readily presented, you have to uncover them. And once you start tracing causes, you start seeing and understanding consequences: the first effect, and then the second, and so on. This skill becomes critical when something new arrives faster than we can understand it, just as AI has in recent years. This leads me to a simple question: Why is the nonprofit sector, of all places, largely unable to trace the negative downstream effects when it comes to AI? To answer this, I start with the last time we fantastically missed the downstream global implications of an emerging technology. In 2012, Facebook went public in what was then the largest tech IPO in US history. Almost nobody priced in what the tech platform would bring with it. Within a few years, pediatricians were tracking cyberbullying patterns that hadn’t previously existed before teenagers carried a 24/7 social feed in their pocket. Schools were writing reactive phone policies that no one needed a few years earlier.

items.title: Are we organizing to save democracy, or build the one we actually need?
items.summary: Executive Director of re:power, Karundi Williams lends her expert opinion on what it will take to build a democracy worth saving. This article was first published in EBONY, and is republished with permission from the author. Right now, much of our political energy is focused on what we fear losing, and that fear is real. Rights that generations fought to secure are being stripped away, so our instinct is understandably to protect what we have. Yet, there is a difference between feeling fear and letting fear determine how we organize. I worry that we have become so focused on saving democracy that we are not spending enough time imagining the democracy we actually need. “Save democracy” is an urgent call, but it is not a big enough vision. When we talk about getting our democracy “back,” we should ask what we are returning to and for whom that version of democracy was actually working. American democracy was not designed for all of us to exercise equal power. Black people had to organize and fight for rights this country deliberately denied us, while women were excluded from political participation for generations. Today, women, immigrants, queer and trans people, and others marginalized in our society are still fighting to hold onto hard-won rights. We should preserve those gains without making restoration our ultimate political aspiration.

items.title: Not just a drop in the bucket
items.summary: The Northern Cheyenne reservation of southeastern Montana is sometimes described as isolated, though it isn't surrounded by water. Whose Movement Is It, a series co-produced by NPQ and the Environmental Justice Oral History Project, is a call to action for those at the forefront of environmental justice decision-making, drawing on insights, hopes, and visions for the future from some of the foundational women organizers of the environmental justice movement. What are the defining characteristics of islands? At their core, they are pieces of land surrounded by water—bounded, set apart, often isolated. The Northern Cheyenne reservation of southeastern Montana is sometimes described the same way, though it isn’t surrounded by water. For the Northern Cheyenne, isolation is not geographic; it is structural, built on decades of uneven access to resources, governance, and political power. The reservation sits surrounded by strip mines, a coal-fired power plant, haulage railroads, and transmission lines. Krystal Two Bulls, Oglala Lakota and Northern Cheyenne, executive director of Honor the Earth and an organizer who grew up on the reservation, has described her frustration with industries capitalizing on the area’s coal reserves at the expense of its water supply. It’s an ongoing fight—one now complicated further by proposals to build a nuclear power plant that could contaminate the clean spring water the tribe’s way of life depends on.

items.title: AI won’t save nonprofits, but it might free them up to save themselves
items.summary: Concerns around AI are valid. Yet, AI is a tool that nonprofit leaders may turn to prepare their organizations to build a more resilient, responsive organization. First: The concerns about artificial intelligence are legitimate. Environmental costs, job displacement, hallucinations, bias baked into training data, the erosion of human connection—all represent genuine, grounded, evidence-based fears we need to address. As mission- and values-driven leaders and organizations, we can’t be expected to leverage any new tools that don’t conform to what we hold most dear, especially when these concerns are likely to be disproportionately felt by the marginalized communities nonprofits exist to serve. Nonprofit leaders and their organizations are being asked to do more with less while the ground shifts beneath them, and the promise is that AI can help. Second: The majority of mission-driven organizations are failing to strategically leverage AI to meet pressing, rapidly expanding demands in these turbulent times. In fact, although 92 percent of nonprofits are using AI in some capacity, the AI Equity Project 2025 survey discovered only about 15 percent currently have an organizational policy for responsible AI use. Of those using AI, an overwhelming majority of nonprofits use it ad hoc, without shared infrastructure or workflows, which means most of the value is being absorbed by individual employees instead of by nonprofits as organizations.

items.title: What the Met museum’s union victory reveals about nonprofit governance
items.summary: The Metropolitan Museum of Art’s union win offers a glimpse into what happens when workers demand that an institution's public commitments also extend to its internal operations. In January 2026, workers at the Metropolitan Museum of Art (the Met) voted by a staggering 76 percent margin to unionize with UAW Local 2110. The union is made up of nearly 900 workers, and this victory offers lessons that other nonprofit leaders can learn from. The museum’s union win is an interesting case study in how employees across departments built a collective voice as they sought better influence over the decisions that ultimately affect them. For nonprofit leaders, boards, and funders, the union win offers a glimpse into what happens when workers demand that an institution’s public commitments also extend to the people running its internal operations. The win didn’t happen overnight. Employees began having conversations about unionizing in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic, then connected in 2022 with UAW Local 2110, a professional (TOP) amalgamated union that represents more than 3,000 white-collar workers. The union campaign brought in museum employees from departments like conservation, curation, library, and information technology.

items.title: Building Scale Before the Curve (Blog)
items.summary: The humble foundation for scaling is often the unimpressive numbers that measure the beginnings of true normative change. Eight percent is a number that will not impress anyone. In our work in Uganda, CARE has digitized 500 savings groups, tracked millions of shillings in loans through a digital platform, and kept portfolio-at-risk below 1 percent. These are the kinds of numbers that headline a program report. But when we decided to look at individual women’s actual behavior—not group performance, not repayment rates, but whether a woman was independently using digital savings or loans on her own—the number we came up with was that one, 8 percent. That number is not scale…at least not yet. But what it is, that’s more important than scale, is real. There has been a lively argument about scale in this publication. Is the social sector’s obsession with scale productive? Is it mostly performative? Does it remain the only honest response to the size of the problems we face? We are not going to settle that argument. But as practitioners who have achieved scale once—with savings groups—and are now trying to do it again in a digital context, we’ve been asking a different question: What does scale actually demand of us before we begin, and who gets left behind when we skip that work?

items.title: Climate Resilience Will Not Be Built by Press Release (Blog)
items.summary: Ahead of COP31, the test for climate finance is no longer what gets announced; it is whether money reaches the systems that protect people. In recent weeks, the climate and development community has moved through a crowded calendar of convenings ahead of COP31, from the UN Climate Week in Baku and Climate Week NYC in September to the pre-COP in Fiji and Tuvalu, Bangkok Climate Action Week, the first-ever Global Heat Forum, the World Bank Group–IMF Annual Meetings in Bangkok, the IPCC plenary in Addis Ababa and the biodiversity COP17 now under way in Yerevan, Armenia. Each of these moments has produced a familiar output of pledges, platforms, hubs and coalitions, announced to applause and then handed to systems that move at a fraction of the speed of the risk they are meant to address. The climate field is already expert in producing declarations, roadmaps, pledges, branded funds and collective statements that generate the appearance of movement while leaving the machinery of escalating harm intact, even as more than three billion people live in contexts highly vulnerable to climate change. Commitments without implementation are not neutral; they function as a form of delay, preserving the appearance of action while leaving the underlying distribution of risk untouched.

items.title: Funding When Democracy Is in Decline (Blog)
items.summary: As the United States joins the ranks of countries with contracting civic space, some lessons from funders with experience working amidst uncertainty. Civic space is rapidly constricting in the United States, as so many organizations can testify. Defined as the environment—both physical and digital—in which people gather to participate in the political, economic, and social life of society, civic space is under threat across the world, of course. But this is increasingly the case as well in the United States. From targeted attacks on nonprofits and lawsuits against media to new federal regulations, cumbersome reporting requirements, and a variety of restrictions on freedoms of assembly, the United States is not immune from the larger trend of democratic decline. However drastic these changes are, they will not be new to funders supporting nonprofit organizations in countries like Russia, Zimbabwe, Venezuela, or Hungary. From inside a major funder that has worked in closed civic spaces for more than 15 years, we’ve learned a great deal about how to meet the moment (sometimes after learning and trying again). Changes to civic space don’t always happen overnight, nor do the consequences: As the instability created leads to isolation, it reduces collaboration and public involvement. It can cause panic and fear, from the largest funder to the smallest nonprofit. Organizations can come to feel like they are taking risks simply by existing, while funders feel vulnerable. And if a funder isn’t adaptable, it only increases grantee isolation and fear.

items.title: Governing Our Data on Our Own Terms (Blog)
items.summary: How one urban Indigenous organization is working to transform data governance using a model that’s founded on Indigenous values For years, nearly every piece of data the Tucson Indian Center (TIC) collected was designed to answer someone else’s questions. Since 1963, TIC has served the urban Native community in Tucson, Arizona, offering primary care and behavioral health services, diabetes prevention and wellness programs, employment and job training, and emergency housing assistance. Intake forms for those programs, satisfaction surveys, and reporting metrics were all developed to collect data that met federal grant requirements but told us almost nothing about what our community wanted to know about itself. Eventually, those of us leading and working at TIC said, “Enough.” We began building a different kind of data system—one organized around our community’s priorities. But to understand why this work is both difficult and transformative requires understanding the origins of contemporary data systems that are used to quantify Native people in the United States.

items.title: How new tech billionaires can save more lives
items.summary: Effective altruism — their go-to giving approach — could do more good by supporting policy changes. A donor who buys bed nets to prevent malaria saves a life for about $5,500, one of the best bargains in philanthropy. But donors who backed advocacy to eliminate trans fat — a toxic food additive — around the globe paid less than $5 per life saved. For some of the world’s deadliest problems, policy change is the royal road to progress. Yet even so, philanthropy too often funds only tangible products and services like vaccines and vitamins. Philanthropists have long debated how to get the best results for the lowest cost. The answer matters even more now because a new generation of donors from AI and other technology companies may soon be in a position to give away tens of billions of dollars a year, and many of them draw on effective altruism, which has favored proven, low-cost approaches to saving lives, such as bed nets. Effective altruism rests on a sound premise: Donations should do as much good as possible. But it could be far more effective if it gave greater priority to policy change. Consider hypertension. A $20 million donation buys a year of medication to prevent heart attacks and strokes for 4 million people at $5 each. That would prevent at least 22,000 heart attacks, strokes, and deaths at less than $1,000 each.

items.title: Drowning in grant proposals? More AI isn’t the only answer
items.summary: Foundations facing an AI-driven flood of grant applications can ask for less, slow down, and keep people in charge of decisions. AI is opening the floodgates for grant proposals as the technology makes it easier for nonprofits to find and apply for more funding opportunities. And the surge is causing a reckoning among program staff at foundations, who face a choice: Use their own AI tools or take longer to respond. A Research on Research Institute analysis from June found applications to research funders have risen roughly 57 percent since ChatGPT came online. Grant makers in other fields say they are seeing a similar trend, particularly for open-call competitions that anyone can apply to. Some funders have started using AI themselves to help expedite the review process, while others argue that the answer isn’t more AI on the review side. The funders and experts the Chronicle interviewed disagree about how much AI is driving the increase, but they largely agree on how to respond. Funders should ask applicants for less, limit the review workload, keep people in charge of reading and deciding, protect applicants’ data, and be open about how AI is used on both sides of the process. The stakes go beyond workload, they say. Funders who handle AI carelessly risk eroding the trust that grant making depends on.

items.title: ‘AI recommends, humans decide’: Circle Foundation’s bet on agentic philanthropy
items.summary: The corporate grant maker is handing its desk work to AI agents so its two leaders can spend more time with grantees. Can an “AI first” grant maker actually have more time for human interaction with grantees? The Circle Foundation intends to find out. The new corporate giving initiative of the Circle Internet Group plans to never have more than two human employees. Instead it will have a much larger team of AI agents that carry out much of the work, said Elisabeth Carpenter, its founding chair. “What we’re looking to do is take the functions and work needed for a foundation and delegate that to AI within a walled garden that’s entirely controlled by humans,” Carpenter said. The Circle Foundation has the advantage of starting from scratch — it was founded a little over a year ago using the 1 percent of shares set aside by its parent, Circle Internet Group, in its June 2025 initial public offering. It plans to give through a donor-advised fund. Also in the works is an in-house “skeptic” agent that is programmed to question decision making and suggest alternate strategies. With AI handling most of the routine tasks, Carpenter and her colleague will have more time to interact with grantees, she said. The organization plans to have quarterly in-person “reporting” calls with partners rather than requiring often-sterile written reports. Transcripts of those calls will then be fed into AI so it can organize the material and make it accessible for ongoing evaluation.

items.title: Podcast: How to build durable community power
items.summary: How a grassroots group founded by immigrant families evolved from an early-education mission into leadership development and more. Is a group that expands its mission from early education to a encompass leadership development, worker-owned cooperatives, and more lacking focus or simply committed to following the community’s needs? In this podcast interview, listen to a discussion on what it takes to fund and lead an organization built around resident-led solutions rather than a single programmatic focus. Hear Phil Buchanan, president of the Center for Effective Philanthropy, talk with Camille Llanes-Fontanilla, Sobrato Philanthropies senior vice president of community impact and systems change and Somos Mayfair’s former longtime executive director, and Saúl Ramos, Somos Mayfair’s current co-executive director. The Chronicle of Philanthropy appreciates the opportunity to share this podcast and wants to note that the interview was conducted by Center for Effective Philanthropy with no involvement from the Chronicle’s newsroom.

items.title: Airbnb pledges $500M for its nonprofit to offer more free emergency stays
items.summary: The group will increase temporary housing support for medical travelers and disaster survivors. Airbnb plans to dedicate $500 million to its philanthropic arm over the next five years to increase temporary housing support for medical travelers and disaster survivors. The short-term rental platform will fund the expansion by donating 10 cents from every booking and make up any shortfall, according to Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky. Airbnb.org, the independent nonprofit whose operating costs are already covered by the company, aims to scale up to eventually provide 1 million nights of free housing each year. The pledge, announced Wednesday, arrives at an uncertain time for corporate philanthropy overall. Most companies reduced their giving over the past five years, according to a recent survey by Chief Executives for Corporate Purpose. Tax law changes have prompted businesses to reconsider their charitable strategies. Airbnb.org’s new funding model has resurfaced questions about the charitable endeavors of a corporation criticized by some affordable housing advocates for worsening the supply of lower-cost, residential housing. The affordable housing crisis — which critics say is exacerbated by Airbnb — means less housing is available for people displaced by disasters. Should a for-profit enterprise use its philanthropy to offset less desirable business impacts? Leading artificial intelligence companies, currently sketching out plans to share some of their wealth, say yes.

items.title: Nonprofits look for a reset following the midterms
items.summary: With Democrats taking over both chambers of Congress, nonprofits want to restore cuts in funding. Nonprofit leaders expressed hope that they would see a normalization of their relationship with the federal government following the landslide election Tuesday in which Democrats took control of both chambers of Congress.That relationship has been tattered by Donald Trump’s second administration. The White House has halted or paused federal grants to charities. Through executive orders, it has forbidden federal support of diversity, equity, and inclusion efforts and programs that support immigrants and LGBTQ people. And it launched or threatened to launch investigations into nonprofits viewed as ideological foes. Akilah Watkins, president of Independent Sector, a network of charities and grant makers, would like to see Congress restore the flow of federal cash to nonprofits that promote research, provide human services, and support education and to safety net programs like nutrition assistance. A new Congress led by Democrats is likely to push for those funding priorities, Watkins said. She and other nonprofit leaders said a Democratic-led Congress will be able to exercise control over federal spending, a responsibility that the current Congress has largely ceded to the Trump administration. “We want to make sure that any interruptions in our funding relationship with the federal government get rectified,” she said.

items.title: After the midterms, democracy funders must not take their foot off the gas
items.summary: Democracy is a long game. Funders would be wise to start acting like it, regardless of who’s in power. Keep up with everything happening in The Commons by signing up for our monthly newsletter. This week’s midterms delivered historic wins for the Democratic Party — and, some would say, for democracy itself. A poll of 80,000 voters in all 50 states found that 32 percent identified the state of democracy as the most important issue facing the country. Widely feared challenges to free and fair elections have not materialized. And in an era of intense polarization, when political allegiances are often assumed to be fixed, the results offer a striking reminder of the dynamism of the American electorate. But funders should be careful not to mistake the results from one election for lasting democratic renewal. I have been in the U.S. democracy space for only a year and a half, but it already feels like a lifetime, given how often we’ve collectively debated, reconsidered, and sometimes radically changed our theories about what it will take to renew democracy. Every major event seems to provoke a strategic reset. Following the 2024 election, we observed a “chill” in democracy funding. As foundations considered the implications of the results, many paused their grant making, launched strategic planning processes, or postponed conversations with grantees.

items.title: Children’s hospital scores $200 million in gifts from two couples
items.summary: Plus, the University of Illinois gets a $100 million pledge, and Marietta College wins a $55 million gift. Two Las Vegas area couples gave big last month to expand pediatric health care in Nevada. Silicon Valley tech investor Ben Horowitz and his wife, Felicia, gave $150 million to Intermountain Health to build Nevada’s first standalone children’s hospital, which will be named for the couple. The health care system also landed a $50 million commitment from Larry and Heidi Canarelli for the planned southwest Las Vegas children’s hospital, and will name one of its towers for the Canarellis. The hospital is scheduled to open in 2030. The Canarellis said in a news release that they are giving the donation because they want to give back to Nevada, where they launched their homebuilding business in the 1980s. Felicia Horowitz, who along with her husband owns a home in Las Vegas, added that “Nevada has a responsibility to create a place where exceptional care and exceptional caregivers come together” to help children and their families. Ben Horowitz co-founded the storied venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, which has invested in more than 1,000 companies including Facebook, Twitter, Lyft, Airbnb, and Coinbase. Forbes pegs his net worth at $18 billion. Larry Canarelli leads Bruin Capital Partners, a real-estate investment firm in Las Vegas. He also founded the Las Vegas homebuilder American West Homes, which he sold to PulteGroup for an estimated $150 million in 2019.

items.title: A food bank targeted donors based on their politics. Here’s what they learned.
items.summary: Some groups are matching their appeals to supporters’ party affiliation, while others stick to shared values. Both are trying to keep everyone giving. Keep up with everything happening in The Commons by signing up for our monthly newsletter. Leaders at the Food Bank of Central & Eastern North Carolina knew that raising money to cover federal funding losses last year was crucial. But they also knew that how they talked about those funding cuts was important: While people across the political spectrum wanted to help those facing food insecurity, the way funding losses were framed could impact whether the message hit home with supporters. “We have all of these different folks, but the one common goal,” says Kendra Paiz, director of the annual fund. “Therefore, we wanted to make sure that we reach everyone in a way that resonates with them.” So Paiz and her team did something an increasing share of nonprofits are trying: They tailored their ask to match readers’ political affinities. In practice, this meant tweaking language and imagery based on how they expected different segments of the population to respond. It also meant keeping close tabs on readers’ reactions in real time. This strategy is one response to a conundrum nonprofits face in 2026: While some want to keep politics as far from their work as possible, they are also finding that donors in an increasingly polarized world want to hear messages that resonate with them and their political leanings.

items.title: Nonprofits and others step in as disaster aid becomes a political lottery
items.summary: The Trump administration denied 26 percent of major disaster declarations in 2025. Four tornadoes tore across southwest Michigan in early March 2026, killing four people. They were the state’s deadliest natural hazards in decades. Gov. Gretchen Whitmer asked the Federal Emergency Management Agency for assistance to cover uninsured and underinsured losses. FEMA said no. She appealed. FEMA said no again. I study how communities prepare for and recover from disasters. As Dean’s Professor of Resilience at Northeastern University, I have written six books on the topic, including the forthcoming “Beyond Common Ground.” The fact that Michigan was repeatedly denied aid reflects a broader shift, one that is putting more weight on the ties between neighbors and the places where they meet. The Trump administration denied 26% of major disaster declarations in 2025, more than double the rate of the year before and well above the 15% denial average of the past two decades. Denials have not fallen evenly. One study looked at some 2,500 disaster declarations since FEMA’s creation in 1979 in states where the governor and U.S. senators were all Republican or all Democrat. In his second term, Trump approved nearly 90% of requests from all-Republican states while approving only 23% of those from all-Democratic states. Colorado, an all-Democratic state, had both of its 2025 appeals for disaster rejected. They were Colorado’s first denials since the 1980s.

items.title: Bringing Routine Vaccines Closer to Children in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC)
items.summary: Routine childhood immunizations, provided on a set schedule over a child’s first two years of life, are very effective at reducing some of the major causes of death in young children. We estimate that in the provinces where we’ve supported programs in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), about one in 13 unvaccinated children dies from vaccine-preventable diseases before the age of five, yet only about half of children there receive the vaccinations they need. Much of our Vaccination research subteam’s work focuses on finding ways to make it easier for caregivers to have their children vaccinated, such as bringing vaccines closer to where parents and infants live. This is especially important in places like DRC, where coverage is low and disease burden is high. Following a request for proposals and a request for information seeking targeted vaccination outreach programs, we funded 11 additional programs, run by distinct organizations—six of which will be implemented in DRC. This portfolio builds on years of investment in our research team, which allowed us to evaluate more than 100 proposals and fund several programs side by side to learn which approaches work best.
